event: He wakes to birdsong; the fire is embers, still warm, the Slate against his chest.
His stomach speaks first: a sharp, insistent hunger that narrows the world to food.
He sits up. The old man is gone, though someone added a log to the fire not long ago.
He goes looking for food; dew turns the morning hillside into a field of small fires.
He shakes an apple tree and three apples fall; he eats one and pockets the others.
He pulls pale-capped mushrooms from a log; the Slate hums and flashes a name he does not know.
A green, long-legged insect lands on his arm; he catches it, cupped, and pockets it.
At the treeline an axe sits buried in a stump; his grip settles on its handle.

changes.note: Link takes the axe left buried in a stump

event: He slides it through his belt beside the bone club: two weapons, neither built for fighting.
Smoke leads him down to a log cabin by a stand of trees, its chimney trailing grey.
Every log in the woodpile is cut to one length and stacked flush: a man making things perfect.
Inside, the old man looks up from a diary in a precise hand: "Ah. You found me."
One room: bed, table, dried herbs; outside, an iron cooking pot hangs over prepared coals.
"You're hungry. Sit. I have ingredients, but no one to cook for."
Link had already dropped an apple, a mushroom and the insect into the hot pot.
It made a grey, rock-hard lump; the Slate gave a flat, short chime and no notice.
He gnaws a piece loose; the Slate shows a full heart restored, but he is still hungry.

changes.note: Dubious food restores a full heart: hearts back to 3/3

event: The old man looks at the pot, then at Link: "There is a recipe in my diary."
Link can read little of the careful, formal hand; one entry lists meat, fish and pepper.
The old man lays out raw meat, a silver bass and three red peppers on a flat stone.
"The trick is knowing what goes together. That is the only magic I know."
Link reaches for the pot; the old man raises a hand: "Not yet. Watch first."
The meat hisses on hot iron, then the fish, then the split peppers.
Lid on: "Patience. The most important ingredient. People rush. Fire doesn't."
They wait as the smell builds in layers: meat, then pepper heat, then sweet fish beneath.
The lid lifts on a golden dish; the Slate chimes: Spicy Meat and Seafood Fry, 4 hearts.
Link eats with his bare hands, too hot, and empties the pot in three handfuls.
The old man's portion sits untouched; he pushes it over: "I don't eat much these days."
Link eats slower now; it is the first meal he has shared with anyone, and it matters.
"You eat as though you're never sure when the next meal is coming."
From a chest by the bed the old man brings a dark blue quilted doublet.
"The mountain to the north gets cold. Cold enough to kill, if you're not prepared."
Link pulls the doublet on over his shirt; it is warm in his hands, and it fits.

changes.note: The old man gives Link the warm doublet

event: "I had it made some time ago. For a traveller I was expecting."
He thinks better of what he meant to say: "The mountain can wait. See other places first."
The Temple of Time stands in the Plateau's centre like a broken hand reaching for the sky.
He crosses knee-high grass and wildflowers and enters under a worn arch twice his height.
A long pillared nave: grass between flagstones, ivy on columns, light through the broken roof.
At the far end stands a pale stone statue of a robed woman, her hands folded in prayer.
He knows nothing of prayer, but he stands straighter, shoulders settled, chin up.
The Slate pulses near her; held up, it shows a dimmed prompt, locked.
He traces words in an old script at her base, understands none, and stays a long time.
"She has been here longer than the Temple," says the old man at the entrance.
He looks at her, raw, a man looking at someone he failed: "Longer than most things."
His hands, folded behind him as if before crowds, clench white, then relax.
His face closes: "There are ruins to the east. Useful things, maybe. Be careful."
East past the temple, through birches lit green and gold, the Eastern Abbey's ruins appear.
Roofless walls, pillars, a courtyard choked with rubble and ivy; he enters, club in hand.
A corroded metal dome lies half-buried, one jointed leg sunk in stone, a black eye on top.
It looks dead, a fossil long past any purpose. He reaches toward it.
The eye ignites a wrong pink-red; the head swivels, precise, and finds him.
Every bird stops singing; a whir builds, and a targeting tone: tik, tik, tik.
A red line runs from the eye to his chest, a warm point tracking him as he breathes.
The Slate shudders a warning against his hip, and the tone speeds up.
He throws himself behind a wall as a blue-white beam blasts it apart, stone and heat on his back.
He runs flat out across the courtyard like an animal; the tone follows, faster.
He dives behind a pillar; the beam cracks it, and he lies flat waiting for the third shot.
It never comes: he is past the arc of the half-buried machine, whose head still watches.
The birds come back one voice at a time; he sits against the stone, hands shaking.
His fingers are locked on the club: four attack, twelve hits, a stick against that dome.
The Plateau is no sanctuary; its walls keep him and the machine in, together.
At the campfire by the temple the old man looks up, sees Link's face, and understands.
He asks nothing; he makes room, and sets the morning's leftovers in a leaf within reach.
Link eats and barely tastes it; the beam has burned a line through his afternoon.
The old man sets a waterskin beside him and turns one log a quarter-turn.
"Those machines cannot be reasoned with. They can barely be fought, not as you are now."
"But the shrines hold tools made to match them. Four shrines, four trials."
He shows the paraglider again: bring what is in all four shrines, and it is Link's.
Link looks east at a shrine's amber glow pulsing in the dark, and nods once.
Something shifts in the old man's face: gratitude, maybe, or grief.
The fire burns low and Link sleeps with the bone club across his lap.
The old man sits formal and upright, as on a throne, and watches him sleep.
He adds a log, precisely. He has waited a hundred years; he can wait one more night.
Grey, cool morning: the old man is already tending the fire, already watching.
Link takes up the bone club, checks the Slate on his hip, and walks toward the shrine.
